MINGORA, Pakistan (CNN) -- Gen. Nadeem Ahmad swirls the helicopter over Pakistan's ground zero. Below is the Swat Valley of North West Frontier Province. A Pakistani soldier patrols a ruined street in Mingora. From the air, the valley in the foothills of the Hindu Kush looks undisturbed. Green fields amid clusters of drab houses. A closer look at Swat reveals how well the Pakistani Army fared in its military campaign to wipe out the militants. The cost of success: massive destruction that is sure to hamper the lives of already suffering residents just starting to trickle back to the homes they fled. A few months ago, ferocious battles between Pakistan's Army and Taliban fighters erupted here -- in Swat, Buner and Lower Dir districts. War's remnants serve as a constant reminder. A destroyed bridge. Pockmarked houses. Hotels that look like they've been abandoned for years. Nadeem maneuvers the chopper to circle Mingora, the largest city in the Swat Valley. From the hilltop Army sentry posts that come into view, soldiers survey the ground below, hard won from Taliban fighters. The militants, Nadeem says, have fled to nearby mountains. On the ground, he shows off a cache of weapons seized in the fighting. The soldiers are keen to boast their victory. Mingora remains on high alert. A curfew has been lifted for morning hours, although soldiers keep close watch on those who venture out. The city's pain is plainly evident on its scarred, deserted streets. Many shops are shuttered or destroyed.  Watch Stan Grant tour the shattered streets of Mingora » . The United Nations estimates that 375,000 Swat Valley residents fled their homes during the fighting. In all, 2.5 million Pakistanis were displaced in what was said to be one of the largest human migrations in recent history. About 260,000 people have been living in 21 refugee camps in neighboring Mardan, Swabi, Nowshera, Peshawar and Charssada districts, but the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees say the "vast majority" of internally displaced Pakistanis have been staying with host families, rented houses or in schools. The government plans to return people first from the camps and then focus on those living elsewhere. But this week, the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) warned that as many as 1 million people could remain displaced until December because of the widespread destruction in their home towns, such as Mingora. Relief agencies have reported dire humanitarian conditions in Mingora: hospitals without electricity that are inundated with patients, an erratic supply of water and natural gas. One resident, who identified himself only as Abdullah, told CNN that returning people are facing shortages in food, water and basic supplies for survival. Some displaced families also expressed concerns about schooling for their children, reported the Integrated Regional Information Networks (IRIN), the U.N. news agency focusing on humanitarian issues. Louis-Georges Arsenault, emergency office director for UNICEF, said 1 million children were at risk of not starting school by September, mainly due to the Taliban's widespread destruction of schools and that 4,000 existing schools continue to shelter displaced people. Businessman Muhammad Khan, 40, who recently returned to Mingora, voiced the despair of returning residents. He told IRIN that "everything is in ruins." "Everything is in ruins," IRIN quoted Khan as saying. "It will take months for life to return to normality." But that normality will no longer include the Taliban, Pakistani soldiers say. The fight was hard, but it was victorious, they say. They point to an area in the city where they say the Taliban displayed the bodies of their victims, some beheaded. It became known as "Slaughter Square." Slaughter Square's name may be outdated for the time being, but residents like Abdullah say it will be a long time before life in Mingora returns to what it once was. "I don't like army. I don't like Taliban," Abdullah says, standing among the ruins of what used to be a thriving market. "I only want peace."

MINGORA, Pakistan (CNN) — Gen. Nadeem Ahmad banks his helicopter above what has become Pakistan’s epicenter of devastation. Beneath him lies the Swat Valley in North West Frontier Province, where a Pakistani soldier walks guard through a wrecked street in Mingora.

Seen from the sky, the valley at the base of the Hindu Kush appears almost untouched: green farmland scattered among groups of dull-colored homes. But a closer view of Swat shows the scale of the Pakistani Army’s campaign against militants — and the heavy price of its success. The fighting left behind extensive damage that is expected to make life even harder for residents who had already suffered and are only beginning to return to the houses they abandoned.

Only months earlier, intense clashes broke out here between Pakistan’s military and Taliban fighters in the districts of Swat, Buner and Lower Dir. Evidence of the war remains everywhere: a collapsed bridge, homes riddled with bullet marks, and hotels that appear to have stood empty for years.

Nadeem guides the helicopter in a circle over Mingora, the biggest city in the Swat Valley. Army lookout posts appear on nearby hilltops, where soldiers keep watch over territory they fought hard to take back from the Taliban. According to Nadeem, the militants have escaped into the surrounding mountains.

Once on the ground, he presents a stockpile of weapons captured during the fighting. The soldiers are eager to highlight their victory.

Even so, Mingora is still under tight security. The curfew has been eased during the morning, but troops closely monitor anyone who comes outside. The suffering of the city is obvious in its empty, damaged streets. Many stores are either closed or ruined.

The United Nations estimates that 375,000 people from the Swat Valley left their homes because of the fighting. Altogether, 2.5 million Pakistanis were forced from their homes in what was described as one of the largest movements of people in recent history.

Around 260,000 people have been staying in 21 refugee camps in the nearby districts of Mardan, Swabi, Nowshera, Peshawar and Charssada. However, the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says the “vast majority” of Pakistan’s internally displaced people have been living with host families, in rented homes or in schools.

The government intends to send people back first from the camps and then turn its attention to those staying in other locations. But this week, the United Nations Children’s Fund, UNICEF, warned that up to 1 million people may remain displaced until December because of the extensive destruction in their hometowns, including Mingora.

Aid organizations have described severe humanitarian problems in Mingora, including hospitals overwhelmed with patients and operating without electricity, along with unreliable supplies of water and natural gas.

One resident, who gave only the name Abdullah, told CNN that people returning home are dealing with shortages of food, water and other basic necessities.

Some displaced families have also raised worries about their children’s education, according to the Integrated Regional Information Networks, or IRIN, the U.N. news agency that covers humanitarian issues.

Louis-Georges Arsenault, UNICEF’s emergency office director, said 1 million children could be at risk of not returning to school by September. He said the main reasons were the Taliban’s widespread destruction of schools and the fact that 4,000 existing schools are still being used to house displaced people.

Muhammad Khan, a 40-year-old businessman who recently came back to Mingora, summed up the hopelessness felt by many returnees. He told IRIN that “everything is in ruins.”

“It will take months for life to return to normality,” IRIN quoted Khan as saying.

Pakistani soldiers insist, however, that any return to normal life will not include the Taliban. They say the battle was difficult but ended in victory. They point to one part of the city where, they say, the Taliban used to display the bodies of their victims, including some who had been beheaded. The area became known as “Slaughter Square.”

For now, that name may no longer apply. But residents such as Abdullah say it will take a long time before Mingora feels the way it once did.

“I don’t like army. I don’t like Taliban,” Abdullah says, standing amid the remains of what was once a busy market. “I only want peace.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news report from Mingora, Pakistan, about the aftermath of the Pakistani Army’s offensive against Taliban militants in the Swat Valley and the challenges facing returning displaced residents.
counterfactuals.output:
**MINGORA, Pakistan —** In the streets of Swat Valley’s largest city, the signs of battle are everywhere: shuttered shops pockmarked by gunfire, homes damaged by shelling, schools standing silent and scarred.

Weeks after Pakistan’s army declared major areas of the valley cleared of Taliban militants, families who fled the fighting are now returning to Mingora and surrounding towns — but many are coming back to uncertainty, destruction and fear.

The military offensive, launched to push Taliban fighters out of Swat, forced hundreds of thousands of civilians from their homes. Many spent weeks in crowded camps or with relatives in other parts of Pakistan’s northwest. Now, as authorities encourage displaced residents to return, the scale of the challenge is becoming clear.

Residents say they are relieved the Taliban’s open presence has been broken, but the return home is not simple. Some neighborhoods still lack reliable electricity and clean water. Markets are slowly reopening, but many businesses have been looted or destroyed. Food prices remain high, and jobs are scarce.

“We came back because this is our home,” one returning resident said, standing outside a damaged house in Mingora. “But we don’t know how we will live. Everything is gone.”

Security remains a major concern. Pakistani soldiers man checkpoints across the city, searching vehicles and questioning travelers. Officials say militants have been killed, captured or driven into the mountains, but many residents fear Taliban fighters may still be hiding among the population or waiting for the army’s presence to ease.

The offensive followed months of Taliban control in parts of Swat, where militants imposed harsh rule, targeted police and government officials, and attacked schools — especially those for girls. The campaign turned the once-popular tourist valley into one of Pakistan’s most visible fronts in the fight against extremism.

For returning families, the damage to education is one of the most painful reminders. Dozens of schools were destroyed or closed during the Taliban’s rise and the subsequent fighting. Parents say they want their children back in classrooms, but many buildings are unsafe or occupied by security forces and relief operations.

Aid agencies are warning that the return process must be handled carefully. They say families need shelter, medical care, cash assistance and protection from unexploded ordnance left behind after weeks of combat. Some displaced residents say they feel pressure to leave camps before their neighborhoods are ready to receive them.

Pakistani officials insist reconstruction is under way and say restoring government authority in Swat is a priority. The army says it will remain in the valley as long as necessary to prevent militants from regrouping.

But for the people of Mingora, victory is measured in more immediate terms: whether the lights come back on, whether the schools reopen, whether the markets recover — and whether they can sleep at night without fear.

For now, Swat is no longer under Taliban control. But the battle to rebuild the valley, and to win back the confidence of its people, has only just begun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed field dispatch describing Gen. Nadeem Ahmad’s helicopter tour over Swat, the destruction in Mingora, refugee conditions, and residents’ fears after the fighting with the Taliban.
counterfactuals.output:
**Field Dispatch: Swat Valley After the Fighting**

**MINGORA, Pakistan —** From the open side of the military helicopter, the Swat Valley looked deceptively calm: green terraces cut into the mountainsides, a pale river winding through the valley floor, and clusters of houses pressed tightly against the slopes. But as the aircraft banked lower over Mingora, the scars of the fighting came sharply into view.

Gen. Nadeem Ahmad, overseeing relief and rehabilitation efforts after the army’s offensive against Taliban militants, studied the landscape from the helicopter as it moved over the valley’s main towns and access roads. Below, whole neighborhoods bore the marks of weeks of combat. Roofs had been blown open. Walls were pocked with bullet holes. Shops that once lined Mingora’s busy bazaars stood shuttered, burned, or crushed by shelling. In some streets, rubble spilled across the road, forcing military vehicles and returning civilians to pick their way carefully through the debris.

The tour offered a stark survey of what the battle for Swat had left behind: a valley emptied, battered, and only slowly beginning to stir back to life.

Mingora, once the commercial heart of Swat, appeared especially damaged. Market stalls were abandoned. Signboards hung twisted above storefronts. Some houses showed signs of direct hits; others had been looted or stripped while their owners fled. The city’s silence was broken by the movement of army patrols, the rumble of trucks carrying supplies, and the occasional appearance of residents who had returned to inspect what remained of their homes.

Gen. Ahmad’s helicopter circled over key areas where the authorities say Taliban fighters had entrenched themselves before being driven out. From the air, the military presence was unmistakable: checkpoints at road junctions, soldiers posted on rooftops, and convoys moving along the main routes into the city. Officials described these positions as necessary to prevent militants from slipping back into the valley, but residents said the sight of armed men — even soldiers — was a reminder that normal life had not yet returned.

Beyond Mingora, the human cost of the fighting was visible in sprawling camps and temporary settlements housing families displaced by the operation. Hundreds of thousands of people from Swat and surrounding districts had fled as the army moved against Taliban positions, many leaving with only clothes, documents, and a few possessions bundled into sacks. In the heat and dust of the camps, families crowded into tents or school buildings converted into shelters.

Conditions remained harsh. Families complained of shortages of clean water, medicine, electricity, and privacy. Aid workers described crowded latrines, long queues for food distributions, and the threat of disease in the summer heat. Parents worried about children who had missed months of school. Men who once ran shops, drove taxis, farmed orchards, or worked as laborers now waited for ration cards and permission to return home.

For many displaced people, the decision to go back was not simple. They wanted to reclaim their homes and fields, but they feared what they might find: unexploded ordnance, destroyed property, missing relatives, or lingering Taliban sympathizers. Some had heard that houses were damaged beyond repair; others feared being accused by one side or the other of collaboration.

“We want to return, but we do not know if it is safe,” was a common refrain among camp residents. Many said they had lived first under Taliban intimidation and then through the terror of bombardment. They were exhausted by both.

Inside Swat, residents who had remained or recently returned spoke quietly of the Taliban’s rule before the army offensive. They recalled public punishments, threats against government workers, attacks on schools — especially girls’ schools — and the forced silence that settled over the valley as militants tightened control. Barbers, musicians, teachers, police officers, tribal elders, and political workers were among those who had lived in fear. Many people said they had stopped speaking openly, afraid that a neighbor, informer, or armed fighter might report them.

Even after the army’s success, that fear had not entirely lifted. Some residents worried that militants had merely shaved their beards, hidden their weapons, or blended back into civilian life. Others feared revenge killings if Taliban fighters returned. There was also anxiety about the behavior of security forces and the possibility of arrests, curfews, or collective suspicion falling on communities trying to rebuild.

The damage to Mingora was not only physical. The fighting disrupted the networks that sustain a city: schools, clinics, courts, markets, transport routes, and local administration. Government officials said restoring these services was essential if the military victory was to hold. Roads had to be cleared, electricity restored, police re-established, and compensation delivered to families whose homes and shops had been destroyed.

Gen. Ahmad’s tour was intended to assess that task as much as to inspect the battlefield. Military and civilian officials accompanying the relief effort emphasized the need for a phased return of displaced families, arguing that people should not be sent back before basic security, food supplies, and sanitation were in place. But the pressure to return was immense. Camps were overcrowded, host families were strained, and many displaced people feared that prolonged absence would cost them their livelihoods.

In Mingora, a few signs of recovery were visible. Some shopkeepers had begun sweeping glass and dust from their storefronts. Families picked through damaged homes, salvaging bedding, cooking pots, and wooden doors. Children watched army trucks pass from alleys and broken courtyards. A handful of vendors reopened stalls, selling tea, bread, and vegetables to soldiers, aid workers, and returning residents.

But the mood remained cautious. Residents spoke in low voices and often looked over their shoulders before discussing the Taliban. Many said they were grateful the militants had been pushed out, but they wanted assurances that the state would not disappear again. Their deepest fear was that the cycle would repeat: the army would leave, the Taliban would return, and civilians would once again be trapped between armed groups.

From the helicopter, the valley’s beauty was still unmistakable. Swat’s mountains rose sharply above the river, and its orchards and fields still stretched across the valley floor. But on the ground, the cost of reclaiming it was evident everywhere — in the shattered homes of Mingora, in the camps full of displaced families, and in the uncertain faces of residents wondering whether peace would last this time.

**Families Return to Ruins After Pakistan’s Swat Offensive**

*By Staff Reporter*  
*Swat Valley, Pakistan —*

Months after Pakistan’s military launched a major campaign to drive Taliban militants from the Swat Valley, thousands of families are returning home to find shattered schools, damaged roads, destroyed markets and a fragile sense of security.

The operation, launched in 2009 after militants tightened their grip on Swat and surrounding areas of Malakand Division, triggered one of Pakistan’s largest internal displacements in recent history. At the height of the crisis, UN agencies and Pakistani officials estimated that more than **2 million people** had fled fighting across Swat, Buner, Lower Dir and nearby districts. Many took shelter with relatives, in rented rooms, or in crowded camps in Mardan, Swabi and other parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

Now, as authorities encourage displaced residents to return, the humanitarian consequences of the conflict are becoming clearer.

“We came back because we had no choice,” said **Rahim Gul**, a shopkeeper returning to Mingora with his family. “But my shop is burned, the shelves are empty, and the school my children went to has no roof. We are home, but life has not returned.”

### Schools Hit Hard

Education has been among the worst affected sectors. Militants had targeted schools—particularly girls’ schools—long before the military operation began, and the fighting compounded the destruction. Humanitarian groups and local education officials reported that **hundreds of schools across Swat and Malakand were damaged or destroyed**, with girls’ schools disproportionately affected.

In some villages, classrooms are unusable, blackboards are broken, furniture is missing, and boundary walls have collapsed. Teachers say attendance remains low because families are struggling to rebuild homes and livelihoods, while some parents fear renewed violence.

“My daughter keeps asking when she can go back to class,” said **Shazia Bibi**, who returned to a village near Matta. “Her school was blown up. The boys are studying in a mosque for now, but there is no place for the girls.”

Officials have promised reconstruction, but residents say rebuilding has been slow. Temporary learning spaces have been set up in some areas, though aid workers warn that a prolonged disruption could push many children—especially girls—out of education permanently.

### Homes, Roads and Markets Damaged

The fighting also left deep scars on civilian infrastructure. Bridges, roads, electricity lines, water channels and health facilities were damaged in several parts of the valley. Markets in towns such as Mingora, Matta and Kabal suffered from shelling, arson and looting, while agricultural communities lost crops, livestock and irrigation networks.

For families returning after months away, the economic toll is severe. Many exhausted their savings while displaced. Others lost the tools of their trades: shop inventories, sewing machines, vehicles, orchards, cattle and farm equipment.

“We found our house standing, but everything inside was gone,” said **Mohammad Ismail**, a farmer from Kabal. “The fields were not watered, the fruit trees were damaged, and our animals disappeared. We survived the fighting, but now we must survive hunger.”

Aid agencies have distributed food, tents, household kits and cash assistance, but many returnees say the help does not cover the scale of losses. In remote villages, access remains difficult because of damaged roads and security restrictions.

### Camps Emptying, Needs Remain

Pakistan’s government has described the return process as a sign of stabilization and military success. Security checkpoints have been set up throughout the valley, and officials say militants have been cleared from many areas.

But humanitarian workers caution that return does not mean recovery. Many families who left displacement camps are moving back to damaged homes without reliable access to clean water, sanitation, electricity, health care or schools.

“The emergency has changed shape,” said one aid worker involved in relief operations. “People are no longer only displaced in camps. They are displaced in their own villages, living among ruins and trying to rebuild without enough resources.”

Health workers also report concerns about trauma, particularly among children who witnessed violence, airstrikes, curfews or the deaths of relatives. Women face additional hardships, including limited access to medical care and restrictions on movement in conservative rural areas.

### Fear Beneath the Surface

While many residents welcome the end of militant rule, fear remains. Some worry that militants may return if governance, policing and reconstruction do not improve quickly. Others are reluctant to speak openly about abuses committed by militants or the impact of military operations, fearing retaliation or official scrutiny.

“We want peace, not just soldiers,” said **Amina Khan**, a mother of five in Mingora. “We want courts, schools, doctors and work. If there is no justice and no livelihood, people will remain afraid.”

For now, Swat’s returning families face the slow task of rebuilding homes and communities in a valley once known for tourism and orchards. The military campaign may have changed the security map, but for civilians, the aftermath is measured in missing classrooms, broken bridges, lost income and children trying to resume normal life amid the debris of war.

**In Mingora, Victory Is Declared Amid Ruins and an Uncertain Return**

**MINGORA, Pakistan** — The army’s trucks rolled through Mingora under a pale mountain sky, past shuttered shops, blown-out storefronts and streets still littered with the remnants of war. Soldiers stood at checkpoints where Taliban gunmen had once enforced their decrees. Loudspeakers that had carried militant threats were silent. On government buildings, Pakistani flags were raised again.

For military commanders, the message was clear: Mingora, the main city of the Swat Valley and once the administrative and commercial heart of the region, had been retaken. After weeks of fighting, the army said it had pushed Taliban militants out of the city and broken their hold over the valley’s most important urban center.

But on the ground, victory looked fragile.

Whole neighborhoods bore the scars of urban combat. Walls were peppered with bullet holes. Electricity poles leaned over empty roads. The fronts of homes had collapsed under shelling. Markets that once drew traders from across Swat were reduced to charred stalls and twisted metal shutters. In side streets, the smell of dust, smoke and rotting food hung in the air. Stray dogs moved through alleys where families had fled in haste, leaving behind bedding, children’s shoes and cooking pots.

The army’s claim of success has opened a new phase in Swat’s crisis — one measured less by battlefield advances than by the slow, dangerous and uncertain return of civilian life.

Military officials said the operation had dealt a decisive blow to the Taliban’s network in Mingora, which militants had used as a base for intimidation, recruitment and attacks. Troops were now conducting house-to-house searches, they said, looking for remaining fighters, weapons caches and roadside bombs. Commanders described the city as largely under government control, though they acknowledged that pockets of resistance and security threats remained.

“We have cleared the main areas,” one officer said near a checkpoint on the road into the city. “The militants have been defeated here. Now our priority is to secure the streets so people can come back.”

That promise is being tested by the scale of the destruction.

Mingora was not merely a battlefield; it was the place where Swat’s collapse into militant rule became visible. Before the fighting, Taliban fighters patrolled openly, set up courts, threatened police and teachers, and imposed harsh restrictions on daily life. Many residents recall the period as one of fear and silence, when anyone accused of opposing the militants risked public punishment or death. Bodies were left in squares as warnings. Girls’ schools were attacked. Music shops were forced to close.

When the military offensive began, most civilians fled. Hundreds of thousands of people from Swat and surrounding areas poured into camps, schools, relatives’ homes and crowded host communities in other parts of Pakistan’s northwest. Their departure emptied Mingora almost overnight.

Now, after the army’s advance, the government faces pressure to show that displaced families can return. Yet relief agencies warn that a premature return could expose civilians to severe risks.

Humanitarian workers say the city lacks reliable electricity, clean water, medical services and functioning markets. Many homes have been damaged or looted. Roads remain difficult to use, and unexploded ordnance may still be present in residential districts. Aid groups also fear that families returning without proper registration or support may find themselves without food, shelter or access to basic care.

“The fighting may have moved on, but that does not mean the crisis is over,” one relief official said. “People need security, water, health services and a way to rebuild their homes. If they return to neighborhoods that are unsafe or unlivable, they may be displaced all over again.”

International and Pakistani aid organizations have urged authorities to allow returns only when conditions are suitable. They say the displaced must be given accurate information about the state of their neighborhoods, the security situation and the availability of assistance. In camps outside the valley, many families say they want to go home but do not know what awaits them.

For residents of Mingora, the desire to return is tangled with fear.

At the edge of the city, a small number of families have begun coming back, traveling in packed vans and trucks loaded with mattresses, plastic water containers and bundles of clothing. Men often arrive first, checking whether houses still stand before calling wives and children to follow. Some find doors broken, cupboards emptied and livestock gone. Others discover that nearby streets are blocked or that their homes sit too close to areas still being searched by troops.

“I wanted to see my house with my own eyes,” said a shopkeeper returning to inspect his property. His storefront, once stocked with household goods, had been damaged by fire. Inside, blackened shelves sagged against the wall. “They say the Taliban are gone. That is good. But how do we start again? Everything here is finished.”

Another resident, walking through a bazaar where metal shutters were scarred by shrapnel, said he had waited for weeks in a relative’s home outside the valley. He returned alone, carrying only a small bag. “My children ask when they can come back,” he said. “I cannot bring them until there is water, electricity and peace. Peace is not just soldiers in the street. Peace is when the market opens and the schools open.”

The army has moved quickly to present its gains as a turning point in the fight against Taliban influence in Pakistan’s northwest. The Swat operation has been framed by officials as proof that the state can reassert control over territory once ceded to militants. For months, the Taliban’s expansion in Swat alarmed Pakistanis and foreign governments alike, especially because the valley lies within reach of major urban centers and had once been known more for tourism than insurgency.

The fall of Mingora to militant influence became a symbol of state weakness. Its recapture is now being promoted as a symbol of state recovery.

Yet the city’s condition shows the costs of that recovery. Schools are closed. Hospitals are strained. Police stations need rebuilding. Local administration must be restored in neighborhoods where militants had replaced government authority with their own system of fear. Residents who cooperated with officials may still fear retaliation from Taliban fighters who escaped into the mountains or blended into the civilian population.

Security remains the central question. The military can control roads and checkpoints, but residents worry about what happens after the troops move on. Many remember earlier moments when authorities announced deals, truces or operations, only for militants to return stronger. For people deciding whether to bring families home, official declarations are not enough.

“We have heard many announcements before,” said a teacher who fled Mingora during the fighting. “This time, we hope it is real. But we will believe it when the courts work, when the police protect people, when girls can go to school without fear.”

Relief agencies say the return process will require careful coordination among the army, civilian authorities and humanitarian groups. The displaced need transportation, food rations, shelter materials and medical support. Children who have spent weeks out of school need classrooms. Families who lost documents during the flight need help accessing aid. Farmers and traders need credit and supplies to restart livelihoods.

There is also the psychological burden of return. Many families fled after living under months of threats and violence. Some witnessed executions or shelling. Children became accustomed to checkpoints, gunfire and sudden displacement. Aid workers say recovery will mean more than clearing rubble; it will require restoring trust in public life.

In parts of Mingora, the silence is broken by military vehicles and the scraping of shopkeepers pulling open damaged shutters. A few men sweep debris from storefronts, though there are few customers. At one intersection, soldiers search cars while boys watch from a distance. Nearby, a mosque loudspeaker calls the faithful to prayer, its voice carrying across streets where entire blocks remain deserted.

The contrast between official confidence and civilian uncertainty is stark. Army spokesmen speak of militants killed, areas cleared and command structures dismantled. Residents speak of missing relatives, ruined businesses and the fear of hidden bombs. Aid groups speak of water systems, sanitation, shelter and the dangers of moving too fast.

All three narratives now define Mingora.

The city has been retaken, but it has not yet recovered. The Taliban’s open presence has been driven out, but the memory of their rule remains embedded in the streets. The army has declared victory, but the return of ordinary life — the reopening of markets, the sound of children in schools, the rebuilding of homes — will come slowly.

For now, Mingora stands in a difficult in-between state: no longer a militant stronghold, not yet a functioning city.

At dusk, soldiers at a checkpoint waved a small convoy through the road leading deeper into Swat. In the back of one truck, a family’s belongings were tied down with rope: a bed frame, a rolled carpet, sacks of grain, a broken chair. A man sitting beside them looked toward the city he had left weeks earlier and was only beginning to reclaim.

“We are going home,” he said. Then, after a pause, he added, “If home is still there.”
